extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, and litigators handling software-implemented inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, prosecuting, and litigating software claim limitations that may invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function / step-plus-function). Focuses on when §112(f) is applied, what must be disclosed in the specification (the corresponding structure/algorithm), and practical drafting/litigation steps to avoid or exploit §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construal under 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation expressed in means-plus-function form 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure ... described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim limitation is treated as means-plus-function under §112(f), the court or examiner will limit the claim to the structure disclosed in the specification that corresponds to the claimed function, and to equivalents of that structure. This construal can materially narrow claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation condition: recitation of 'means' or 'step' or generic placeholder
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim limitation recites the term 'means' (or 'step') or a generic placeholder (e.g., mechanism, module, device, unit, component, element, member, apparatus, machine, system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the word 'means' or similarly generic nouns/labels for an element is a trigger for §112(f). The page explicitly lists examples of generic placeholders to watch for: mechanism, module, device, unit, component, element, member, apparatus, machine, system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation condition: functional language modification
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is modified by functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the element is described primarily by what it does (i.e., functional language) rather than by concrete structure, that functional modification supports applying §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation condition: absence of sufficient structure/material/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is not modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for performing the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a non-'means' term is used, §112(f) will be invoked when the claim lacks sufficient structural or physical detail (structure, materials, or specific acts) that perform the recited function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure requirement — algorithm for computer-implemented functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once §112(f) is invoked, the specification must describe the 'structure' that corresponds to that function; for computer-implemented functions, 'the corresponding structure ... for a computer-implemented function is the algorithm disclosed in the specification.' (Aristocrat Tech. Aus. Pty Ltd v. Int’l Game Tech.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required corresponding structure is not satisfied by merely naming a generic computer or microprocessor. The specification must disclose an algorithm (or equivalent sufficient structural detail) that performs the claimed function; otherwise the claim lacks the necessary corresponding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of failing to disclose corresponding structure (indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to disclose the structure that performs the claimed function renders the claim invalid for indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not provide sufficient corresponding structure (e.g., an algorithm for a software function), courts or examiners may find the claim indefinite under §112 and invalidate or reject it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting best practice: avoid generic placeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting a claim, avoid the §112(f) trap by avoiding generic placeholders, e.g. 'a software module comprising software instructions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on generic labels like 'module' or 'mechanism' without describing structure. Instead, explicitly describe the substeps, operations, data structures, or other structural features that implement the function so the claim element is tied to sufficient structure rather than pure function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting best practice: include algorithmic substeps or sufficient structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify each element with applicable substeps in sufficient detail to accurately describe the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent §112(f) treatment, draft claim elements to recite concrete substeps, specific acts, or structural features that show how the function is performed (i.e., the algorithmic implementation), rather than only high-level functional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation/vetting practice: look for §112(f) and algorithm disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When litigating, look for the §112(f) issue and whether the specification explicitly describes an algorithm or some way to program a computer/processor to perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a litigation or clearance strategy, examine claims for triggers (means/generic placeholders, purely functional language, lack of structure) and analyze the specification for corresponding algorithmic disclosure; these points may be used to narrow or invalidate claims or to defend against indefiniteness arguments.
